lesson.title: Steady state plus a dying transient

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the shaded gap to the steady line shrinking to 0.368 of itself at every τ mark when you drag the time marker along a coil's switched-on current.
interactive.title: The steady line and the gap
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: This is a short lesson in fourteen small screens, all on one plot. A 24 V DC supply, a switch, a 0.5 H coil and a 10 Ω resistor sit in one loop. The loop is drawn small beside the plot. Current runs up the side, from 0 to 4 A. Time runs along the bottom, from 0 to 0.3 s. The voltages round the loop add up, so 24 = L di/dt + R i. The resistor takes 10 i volts. The coil takes the rest. So di/dt = (24 − 10 i) ÷ 0.5. The current climbs fast at first. It slows as the resistor takes more of the supply. A dashed line marks the steady current, E ÷ R = 2.4 A. At that current the coil's share is zero, so the rate is zero too. The gap between the line and the current is shaded. Call it g = i − 2.4. It is negative below the line. While the supply holds, the steady value does not move. So the gap changes as fast as the current does. The rule then reads dg/dt = −g ÷ 0.05. That is the decay rule of the discharge. So the gap keeps 0.368 of itself in every τ = L ÷ R = 0.05 s. A mark sits at each τ along the bottom. Here is each screen in turn. Screen 1 closes the switch first. Then the curve grows behind a rider. The current rises from 0 at 48 A a second. It bends over towards the dashed line. Screen 2 asks what current makes the rate zero. The choices are 2.4 A, 240 A or 48 A. Screen 3 draws the dashed line at 2.4 A, the steady state, and shades the gap. It rewrites the rule as di/dt = (2.4 − i) ÷ 0.05. The 0.05 s is 0.5 ÷ 10, which is L ÷ R. So the rate is in proportion to the gap. Rate arrows sit at 0 A and at 1.2 A. They show the rate halving as the gap halves. Screen 4 asks the rate when the current is 1.2 A. The choices are 24 A a second, 48 A a second or 1.2 A a second. Screen 5 gives the reason the gap decays. The steady line holds still, so the gap obeys the discharge's rule. So each τ keeps the same share of it. The screen lets you drag a time marker along the curve. As it moves, readouts show the time, the current and the gap. A fourth readout shows the gap ÷ the gap one τ earlier. At the τ marks the gap reads −2.4, −0.883, −0.325 and −0.119 A. So the ratio holds at 0.368. The current reads 0, 1.52, 2.08 and 2.28 A. At five τ, which is 0.25 s, it reads 2.38 A. A rate arrow rides with the marker. Its slope is the gap ÷ τ. So it flattens as the gap shrinks. A straight tangent at the starting rate meets the dashed line at one τ. On a phone the four readouts wrap onto two lines. Screen 6 asks the current after one τ, which is 0.05 s. The choices are 1.52 A, 2.4 A or 0.883 A. Screen 7 presses Split. The curve comes apart into two pieces. One is the flat steady line at 2.4 A. The other is the dying gap, −2.4 e^(−t/0.05), drawn below the axis. On that screen the current axis runs from −2.5 to 4 A. Add the two, height by height, and you get the current back. So i = 2.4 − 2.4 e^(−t/0.05). The screen adds that with a sine supply the steady part is a sine. For a resistor and capacitor it is what the impedance method gives. Screen 8 shows a second route, the integrating factor. Three lines of working appear: di/dt + i ÷ 0.05 = 48, then the slope of i e^(t/0.05) is 48 e^(t/0.05), then i e^(t/0.05) = 2.4 e^(t/0.05) + c. The start of 0 A gives c = −2.4. Then the same curve draws in. Screen 9 starts with the current steady at 2.4 A. Then it drops the supply to 12 V. The new dashed line sits at 1.2 A. The gap starts at +1.2 A above it. It asks which formula the current now follows. The choices are i = 1.2 + 1.2 e^(−t/0.05), i = 1.2 (1 − e^(−t/0.05)) or i = 2.4 e^(−t/0.05). A wrong pick is drawn too. That shows where it starts or ends in the wrong place. Screen 10 opens three sliders and a switch. E runs from 6 to 30 V. R runs from 10 to 20 Ω. The starting current runs from 0 to 4 A. E and R move the dashed line. R also changes τ. The start moves only the gap. It can sit above or below the line. Flip the two-way switch mid-run and the supply drops out. The loop then closes through R. The dashed line drops to 0. The coil's current dies as a discharge does. Whatever the settings, the gap keeps 0.368 of itself from one τ mark to the next. The one exception is across a switch flip, because the line jumps there. Screen 11 asks what changes with a 1 H coil in place of the 0.5 H one. The choices are the same 2.4 A reached more slowly, a steady 1.2 A, or a steady 4.8 A. Screen 12 swaps the skin. A named choice offers Coil, Motor and Tank. Each skin draws time in τ. It draws the value as its share of the way from its start to its steady value. So all three draw one curve. The tank fills from empty, with its outflow in step with its level. A ship answering its rudder is named as one more case. It is 63.2% of the way at one τ, 86.5% at two, 95.0% at three and 99.3% at five. Screens 13 and 14 mix it all. Screen 13 takes a motor whose speed n obeys dn/dt = (1500 − n) ÷ 0.2, in rpm and seconds. The motor starts from rest. The screen asks its speed after 0.4 s. The choices are 1297 rpm, 1500 rpm or 203 rpm. Screen 14 takes a tank whose level h obeys dh/dt = (2 − h) ÷ 50, in metres and seconds. The level starts at 3 m. The screen asks the level after 50 s. The choices are 2.37 m, 1.10 m or 2.63 m. Each puzzle offers three answers.
interactive.ignores: The coil is ideal. Its L stays fixed. It has no capacitance of its own. The 10 Ω includes the coil's own winding. The switch acts at once, with no arc. The run is slowed down, so 0.3 s plays over a few seconds. Near 0.3 s the current looks as if it touches 2.4 A. By this rule it never quite does. The motor and tank rules are example rules. A real motor's run-up depends on its load. A tank draining freely through a hole follows a different rule. So its curve is not this exact shape.

explain.text:
Switch a coil onto a supply and its current climbs to a steady value, E ÷ R. On the way, the current is that steady value plus a gap. The gap dies away just as a discharge does.

Take a 24 V supply, a 0.5 H coil and 10 Ω in series. Round the loop the voltages add up: E = L di/dt + R i. The resistor takes R i. The coil takes the rest. At switch-on the current is 0, so all 24 V sits across the coil. That gives di/dt = 24 ÷ 0.5 = 48 A a second. As the current grows, the resistor takes more. That leaves the coil less, so the rise slows. It stops when the coil's share reaches zero. Set di/dt = 0 and you get 24 = 10 i, so i = 2.4 A. That is the steady state, E ÷ R.[^1] Only the supply and the resistance set it. L does not appear in it.

Now the key step. Divide the rule by L, and di/dt = (E − R i) ÷ L. Take R out of the top, and di/dt = (E ÷ R − i) ÷ (L ÷ R). The top is how far the current is from its steady value. So the rate is in proportion to that gap. Call the gap g = i − E ÷ R. Below the line g is negative. While the supply holds, E ÷ R does not move. So the gap changes exactly as fast as the current. That gives dg/dt = −g ÷ τ, with τ = L ÷ R.[^2] This is the decay rule you separated and integrated. So g = g₀ e^(−t/τ), where g₀ is the gap at the start. Here τ = 0.5 ÷ 10 = 0.05 s and g₀ = −2.4 A. Each τ keeps 0.368 of the gap. It goes −2.4 A, then −0.883 A, then −0.325 A. So the current reads 1.52 A after one τ and 2.08 A after two. Put the other way, each τ closes 0.632 of what is left. By this rule the gap never quite reaches zero. After five τ, which is 0.25 s, the current reads 2.38 A. That is 99.3% of the way.

Put together, i = E ÷ R + (i₀ − E ÷ R) e^(−t/τ). The first part is the steady state. The supply and R set it. The second part is the [[transient]]. Where the current starts sets it, and it dies away. More L with the same R changes only τ. The same rule holds if the current starts above the line. It also holds if the supply drops mid-run. Each time there is a new gap, timed from that moment. A damped spring pushed by a force splits the same way. It has a transient that depends on the start, plus a steady state set by the push, not by the start. A ship answering its rudder is often modelled the same way, with a gain K and a time constant T.[^4] With a sine supply the steady part is a sine wave. For a resistor and capacitor it is exactly what the impedance method gives.[^5] All of this assumes an ideal coil whose L stays fixed.

**Switched onto a supply, a coil's current is the steady value E ÷ R plus a gap that dies as e^(−t/τ), with τ = L ÷ R. The supply and R set the steady value. The start sets the gap.**

analogy.text: Put a steady load on a cable and it warms towards a running temperature. That load sets the temperature. The further below it the cable is, the faster it climbs. So in a simple picture it closes the same fraction of the gap in each equal time. A cable that starts warm just starts with a smaller gap.
analogy.breaks: A real cable's resistance rises as it warms. So a steady load's heat creeps up as it goes. Its curve is only roughly this shape.

practice.text:
**Safe way first:** a coil's voltage is L di/dt. Break its current suddenly and di/dt is huge. So the voltage across the coil spikes. So plan for that spike whenever a coil's current is cut.

- Write the rule as rate = (steady value − value) ÷ τ.
- Find the steady value by setting the rate to zero. For a coil it is E ÷ R.
- Find τ. For a coil it is L ÷ R, in seconds.
- Find the starting gap. It is the start value minus the steady value.
- Write value = steady value + starting gap × e^(−t/τ).
- Check the start. At t = 0 it gives the start value.
- Check the end. As t grows it settles on the steady value.
- Put it back into the rule to check the slope.

**Rule of thumb:** each τ keeps 0.368 of the gap and closes 0.632 of it. After five τ about 0.7% of the starting gap is left.

**Worked example:** say a coil of 2.2 H and 55 Ω goes onto 110 V DC. The steady current is 110 ÷ 55 = 2 A. The time constant is τ = 2.2 ÷ 55 = 0.04 s. The current starts from 0, so the starting gap is −2 A. So i = 2 − 2 e^(−t/0.04). Its starting rate is 110 ÷ 2.2 = 50 A a second. After 0.04 s it reads 2 − 2 × 0.368 = 1.26 A. After 0.08 s it reads 1.73 A. After 0.2 s it reads 1.99 A.

**Another route, the integrating factor:** first put the rule in standard form, with di/dt on its own. That gives di/dt + i ÷ τ = E ÷ L. Now multiply both sides by e^(t/τ). The aim is a left side that is the slope of one thing. Two facts make that work. First, e^(t/τ) grows in proportion to itself. So its slope is e^(t/τ) ÷ τ. That is the decay rule with a plus sign. Second, the slope of a product. Picture i × e^(t/τ) as the area of a rectangle. In a short time each side grows a little. The area gains a strip along each side, plus a tiny corner that shrinks away. So the slope of i e^(t/τ) is di/dt × e^(t/τ) + i × e^(t/τ) ÷ τ. That is the left side times e^(t/τ). So the slope of i e^(t/τ) is (E ÷ L) e^(t/τ). Now go back from slopes to the things themselves. The thing whose slope is e^(t/τ) is τ e^(t/τ). So i e^(t/τ) = (E ÷ L) τ e^(t/τ) + c. Here (E ÷ L) × τ is E ÷ R. Divide by e^(t/τ) to get i = E ÷ R + c e^(−t/τ). The start sets c = i₀ − E ÷ R. It is the same answer.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading τ as the time to reach the steady value. After one τ, 0.368 of the gap is still there.
- Using i = E ÷ R × (1 − e^(−t/τ)) when the current does not start at 0. Use the start to find the gap.
- Mixing up the fraction kept and the fraction closed. Each τ keeps 0.368 of the gap and closes 0.632.
- Expecting more L alone to change the final current. With R the same, L sets only τ.
- Expecting a falling current to go to zero. It settles on the new steady value.

interactive.html:
A 24 V supply switches onto a 0.5 H coil and 10 Ω, and the current climbs to a steady line. Every value is an example.

Every curve, gap and reading is worked out from the rule on its screen.
interactive.title: The steady line and the gap
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the shaded gap to the steady line shrinking to 0.368 of itself at every τ mark when you drag the time marker along a coil's switched-on current.

checks.label: The initial current is zero and approaches V ÷ R with a characteristic time constant: from a start of 0 A the curve climbs towards a steady line drawn at E ÷ R, always below it and rising, for every E and R on the sliders
The time constant for an RL circuit is τ = L ÷ R: the τ marks sit L ÷ R apart for every R on the slider, 0.05 s for 0.5 H and 10 Ω, and the 1 H coil keeps 0.368 of its gap at 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1 s

0.632 of the remainder is achieved in every characteristic time, and the final value is never exactly reached: from one τ mark to the next the gap keeps 0.368 of itself for every E, R and start on the sliders, with the supply on or flipped, and no gap reaches zero

The general solution is a transient that depends on the start plus a steady state independent of it: split, the steady line plus the dying gap gives the current at every time, and on the sliders the start changes only the gap, never the steady line

Along the marker: at the τ marks the gap reads −2.4, −0.883, −0.325 and −0.119 A and the current 0, 1.52, 2.08 and 2.28 A, then 2.38 A at 0.25 s; from 0.05 s on, the gap ÷ the gap one τ before reads 0.368 wherever the marker sits; the rate arrow's slope is the gap's size ÷ τ; the starting rate's line meets the steady line at one τ

Every worked number is right: 2.4 A steady, τ = 0.05 s, 48 A a second at the start and 240 for the slip, 24 A a second at 1.2 A, 0.368 kept and 0.632 closed, 1.52 A and 0.883 A after one τ, 1.2 A steady at 12 V with a +1.2 A start gap, 3 A and 0.025 s at the slider ends, 0.1 s for 1 H with the slips 1.2 and 4.8 A, 63.2, 86.5, 95.0 and 99.3% for every skin, 1297 and 203 rpm, 2.37, 1.10 and 2.63 m, and 0.7% left after five τ
Each puzzle accepts only its answer, draws it when it is checked, and draws every wrong pick as a mistake
Before Check, no puzzle's picture shows its answer or a mistake
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, finishes within 2 s

applied.problem: It says a bigger coil changes only τ and the input alone sets the steady value; a real bigger coil usually has more winding resistance, E ÷ R depends on R, and after i7 a pushed spring's steady swing depends on the system too, not only the push (the quote says independent of the start).

The mistake 'expecting a bigger coil to change the final current' is often right in real life, since a bigger coil usually has more winding resistance; only more L with the same R leaves E ÷ R unchanged.

Screen 9's 'whatever the settings, 0.368 at every τ mark' fails across a mid-run switch flip, where the steady line and gap jump; and screen 11's 'percentage of its steady value' matches 63.2% at one τ only for a start from zero, while 'share of the way' holds for any start.
